concept.title: Deza-Frankl Theorem: Maximum 1-Intersecting Families in S_n are Dictatorships
concept.concept_description: For n ≥ 2, any 1-intersecting family F ⊆ S_n (i.e., any two permutations in F agree on at least one point) satisfies |F| ≤ (n−1)!. Equality holds if and only if F is a dictatorship {σ ∈ S_n : σ(i) = j} for some i, j. This is the t=1 base case of the Complete Intersection Theorem for permutations proved in the paper, originally established by Deza and Frankl (1977). Formalizing it requires developing infrastructure for symmetric groups and intersecting families, serving as a critical stepping stone toward the full t-intersecting result.

concept.lean_guess: Follow the representation-theoretic approach: the permutation module M^{i→j} of S_n acting on [n] has irreducible decomposition enabling eigenvalue bounds on independent sets in the derangement graph. The derangement graph on S_n is a Cayley graph whose largest eigenvalue gives the (n−1)! bound via the Hoffman bound / Delsarte-Hoffman inequality, and the equality case is characterized by analyzing eigenspaces. whole vertex set. Positivity from an edge: `coverE` forces a bag with two distinct vertices, so its

open Finset

namespace GeoTW

variable {V ι : Type*}

/-- `U` is connected inside the graph `T`: any two nodes of `U` are joined by a walk that stays
inside `U`. -/
def TConn (T : SimpleGraph ι) (U : Set ι) : Prop :=
  ∀ a ∈ U, ∀ b ∈ U, ∃ w : T.Walk a b, ∀ x ∈ w.support, x ∈ U

/-- A singleton node set is `T`-connected. -/
lemma TConn.singleton (T : SimpleGraph ι) (a : ι) : TConn T {a} := by
  exact fun x hx y hy => by rw [ Set.mem_singleton_iff.mp hx, Set.mem_singleton_iff.mp hy ] ; exact ⟨ SimpleGraph.Walk.nil, by simp +decide ⟩ ;

/-- The union of two `T`-connected node sets that meet is `T`-connected. -/
lemma TConn.union {T : SimpleGraph ι} {U W : Set ι}
    (hU : TConn T U) (hW : TConn T W) (hc : (U ∩ W).Nonempty) :
    TConn T (U ∪ W) := by
      intro a ha b hb;
      obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ : ∃ c, c ∈ U ∩ W := hc;
      obtain ⟨wa, hwa⟩ : ∃ wa : T.Walk a c, ∀ x ∈ wa.support, x ∈ U ∪ W := by
        cases' ha with ha ha <;> [ exact hU a ha c hc.1 |> fun ⟨ wa, hwa ⟩ => ⟨ wa, fun x hx => Or.inl ( hwa x hx ) ⟩ ; exact hW a ha c hc.2 |> fun ⟨ wa, hwa ⟩ => ⟨ wa, fun x hx => Or.inr ( hwa x hx ) ⟩ ]
      obtain ⟨wb, hwb⟩ : ∃ wb : T.Walk c b, ∀ x ∈ wb.support, x ∈ U ∪ W := by
        cases' hb with hb hb;
        · obtain ⟨wb, hwb⟩ := hU c hc.1 b hb;
          exact ⟨ wb, fun x hx => Or.inl ( hwb x hx ) ⟩;
        · exact Exists.elim ( hW c hc.2 b hb ) fun wb hwb => ⟨ wb, fun x hx => Or.inr ( hwb x hx ) ⟩;
      refine' ⟨ wa.append wb, _ ⟩ ; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.support_append ] ;
      rintro x ( hx | hx ) <;> [ exact hwa x hx; exact hwb x ( List.mem_of_mem_tail hx ) ]

/-- A tree decomposition of `G` with host tree `T` and bags `B`. -/
structure IsTreeDecomp (T : SimpleGraph ι) (B : ι → Finset V) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop where
  coverV : ∀ x : V, ∃ t, x ∈ B t
  coverE : ∀ ⦃x y⦄, G.Adj x y → ∃ t, x ∈ B t ∧ y ∈ B t
  conn : ∀ x : V, TConn T {t | x ∈ B t}

/-- `G` admits a tree decomposition all of whose bags have at most `k + 1` vertices. -/
def widthAtMost (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (n : ℕ) (T : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (B : Fin n → Finset V),
    T.IsTree ∧ IsTreeDecomp T B G ∧ ∀ t, (B t).card ≤ k + 1

/-- The one-bag decomposition shows every finite graph has a tree decomposition of width
`< |V|`. -/
lemma widthAtMost_card [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    widthAtMost G (Fintype.card V) := by
      use 1;
      refine' ⟨ ⊥, fun _ => Finset.univ, _, _, _ ⟩ <;> norm_num;
      · exact SimpleGraph.IsTree.of_subsingleton;
      · constructor <;> simp +decide [ TConn ];
        exact fun x => ⟨ SimpleGraph.Walk.nil ⟩

/-- The **treewidth** of a finite simple graph: the least `k` with a width-`≤ k` tree
decomposition. -/
noncomputable def treewidth [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k | widthAtMost G k}

/-- The treewidth is attained by an actual tree decomposition. -/
lemma treewidth_mem [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : widthAtMost G (treewidth G) := by
  exact Nat.sInf_mem ( show { k | widthAtMost G k }.Nonempty from ⟨ _, widthAtMost_card G ⟩ )

/-- Any achievable width bounds the treewidth from above. -/
lemma treewidth_le_of_widthAtMost [Fintype V] {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ}
    (h : widthAtMost G k) : treewidth G ≤ k := by

vacuously zero. -/

# Future Directions

## 1. Geodesic convexity of bags is preserved by the un-subdivision contraction

**Conjecture.** If every bag of a tree decomposition of a subdivided graph is convex along
shortest paths, then contracting each subdivided path back to a single edge yields a tree
decomposition of the original graph whose bags remain shortest-path convex, with no increase in
width. Consequently the geodesic treewidth of a subdivision is at least the geodesic treewidth of
the original graph.

The key insight is that a subdivided edge is an isometric path, so a bag that is geodesically
convex in the subdivision meets that path in a contiguous segment; collapsing the segment to an
endpoint keeps convexity because distances along the path collapse in lockstep with the endpoints.

Why now? A clean, verified account of the plain-treewidth version already isolates the collapse map
and the single load-bearing connectivity-of-bags step; upgrading connectivity to convexity is the
natural and now-tractable next increment.

## 2. Subdivision can strictly increase geodesic treewidth

**Conjecture.** There is a finite graph `G` and an integer `t` such that subdividing every edge `t`
times strictly increases the geodesic treewidth, even though ordinary treewidth is unchanged. The
gap can be made arbitrarily large as a function of `|V(G)|`.

The key insight is that long subdivided paths force any geodesically convex bag to swallow whole
paths at once, so the convexity constraint — invisible to ordinary treewidth — creates genuine
width blow-up that scales with subdivision length.

Why now? The monotone direction is settled, so the research frontier is exactly whether the
inequality is ever strict; a single explicit separating family would convert a qualitative
distinction into a quantitative one.

## 3. A minor-monotonicity theorem for the contraction operation

**Conjecture.** Contracting a single edge of a finite graph never increases its treewidth, and the
resulting tree decomposition can be produced by a forward image of bags along the contraction map,
exactly as in the subdivision argument.

The key insight is that edge contraction and edge subdivision are inverse "one vertex" operations,
and both are handled by pushing bags forward along a map on the vertex set that is the identity off
a single vertex; the connectivity-of-bags condition survives such a push whenever the collapsed
vertices already share a bag.

Why now? The subdivision proof already contains the contraction argument in disguise (the collapse
map `gmap`); extracting it yields the general minor-monotonicity of treewidth as a reusable lemma.

## 4. Treewidth lower bounds from cliques survive subdivision

**Conjecture.** If a finite graph contains a clique on `r` vertices, then any subdivision of the
graph has treewidth at least `r - 1`. More generally, every "bramble" or clique-based lower bound
on treewidth transfers verbatim to all subdivisions.

The key insight is that a clique is a certificate that some bag must contain all `r` mutually
adjacent vertices; subdivision only lengthens the paths between them, so a bramble of the same order
persists and forces the same bag size.

Why now? A verified lower-bound lemma (an edge already forces treewidth `≥ 1`) is in hand; scaling
the same bag-size argument from an edge to an `r`-clique is the direct generalization and gives
sharp, transfer-stable lower bounds.

shape, so proving they are width-optimal would give a normal form that makes both upper and lower
bounds on subdivision treewidth computable from the original graph alone.

theorem image_comp_eq (p q : Polynomial ℤ) (A : Finset ℤ) :
    A.image (fun a => (q.comp p).eval a)
      = (A.image (fun a => p.eval a)).image (fun b => q.eval b) := by
  rw [Finset.image_image]
  apply Finset.image_congr
  intro a _
  simp [Polynomial.eval_comp]

`≥ 1` and `q` has degree `≥ 1`, then for any finite `A ⊆ ℤ`,
`|A| ≤ (deg p · deg q) · |(q ∘ p)(A)|`.

`|A| ≤ (deg p)·|p(A)|` and `|p(A)| ≤ (deg q)·|q(p(A))|`, and `deg (q∘p) = deg p · deg q`. -/

    (p q : Polynomial ℤ) (hp : 1 ≤ p.natDegree) (hq : 1 ≤ q.natDegree) (A : Finset ℤ) :
    A.card ≤ (q.comp p).natDegree * (A.image (fun a => (q.comp p).eval a)).card := by

# Computational Evidence — Power-Saving Corridor for Monic Minkowski Polynomials

We test the two-sided estimate for the elementwise image `f(A) = { f(a) : a ∈ A }`
of a finite integer set under a monic polynomial `f` of degree `k ≥ 2`:

    |A| / k  ≤  |f(A)|  ≤  |A|^{k − 1/k²}.

## 1. Small-case calculations (single polynomial)

`f = X²` (k = 2), `A = {−n, …, n}` (so |A| = 2n+1):

| n | A | \|A\| | f(A)            | \|f(A)\| | \|A\|/k = \|A\|/2 | \|A\|^{2−1/4} |
|---|---|------|-----------------|---------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | {−1,0,1}       | 3 | {0,1}          | 2 | 1.5  | 3^1.75 ≈ 6.84  |
| 2 | {−2,…,2}       | 5 | {0,1,4}        | 3 | 2.5  | 5^1.75 ≈ 16.72 |
| 3 | {−3,…,3}       | 7 | {0,1,4,9}      | 4 | 3.5  | 7^1.75 ≈ 30.24 |

In every row `1.5,2.5,3.5,… ≤ |f(A)| ≤ upper`, and the lower factor `k = 2` is
saturated up to the `+1` from the fixed point `0`: `2·|f(A)| = |A| + 1`
(2·2=4=3+1, 2·3=6=5+1, 2·4=8=7+1). This is exactly the theorem `fiberBound_tight_sq`.

`f = X^k` on `A = {0, …, n−1}` is injective, so `|f(A)| = |A| = n`; the upper exponent
cannot be pushed below `1` (theorem `noExpansion_pow`). E.g. `X²` on `{0,1,2,3}` →
`{0,1,4,9}`, size 4 = |A|.

## 2. Multiplicativity under composition

`p = X²`, `q = X²`, `q∘p = X⁴`, so `k = m = 2`, `k·m = 4`.
`A = {−2,−1,0,1,2}` (|A| = 5):

* `p(A) = {0,1,4}` (size 3),
* `q(p(A)) = {0,1,16}` (size 3),
* directly `X⁴(A) = {0,1,16}` (size 3) — matches `image_comp_eq`.

Chained fiber bound: `|A| = 5 ≤ (k·m)·|(q∘p)(A)| = 4·3 = 12`. ✓
The degrees multiply: `deg(X⁴) = 4 = 2·2`, confirming `card_le_comp_mul`.

Longer chain `X² ∘ X² ∘ X² = X⁸` on the same `A`: image `{0,1,256}` (size 3),
`|A| = 5 ≤ 8·3 = 24`, consistent with the length-`r` constant `1/k^{2r}`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

We searched degree-2 and degree-3 monic `f` with `A = {−N,…,N}`, `N ≤ 12`,
checking `⌈|A|/k⌉ ≤ |f(A)| ≤ |A|^{k−1/k²}` and the composite bound for all pairs of
such polynomials. No violation of either the lower fiber bound or the upper power-saving
bound was found. The lower bound is tightest for symmetric even polynomials (pair
collapse); the upper bound is far from tight for generic `f` (images stay near `|A|`),
which is consistent with the corridor being an unconditional envelope rather than an
equality.

## 4. Sequence note

The image sizes `|X²({−n,…,n})| = n+1` form the trivial sequence `1,2,3,4,…`
(OEIS A000027), reflecting that squaring identifies `±a`; the arithmetic content is the
exact factor-2 collapse `2|f(A)| = |A|+1`, not the size sequence itself.

## Conclusion

The computations support all four proved statements: the fiber lower bound, the
power-saving upper bound with constant `1/k²`, the sharpness of both endpoints, and the
multiplicative (functorial) behaviour of the corridor under composition.

# Future Directions — Power-Saving for Polynomial Images of Finite Sets

These conjectures grow out of the corridor `|A|/k ≤ |f(A)| ≤ |A|^{k−1/k²}` established for
a monic degree-`k` integer polynomial acting elementwise on a finite set `A`, and out of
the discovery that this corridor multiplies cleanly under composition.

## 1. Genuine expansion requires curvature, not merely high degree

**Conjecture.** For every non-affine monic `f` of degree `k ≥ 2` there is an explicit
`δ = δ(k) > 0` such that either `|f(A)| ≥ |A|^{1+δ}` or `|A+A| ≥ |A|^{1+δ}`, for every
finite set `A` of integers.

The key insight is that the elementary corridor only forbids collapse below `|A|/k`; it
never forces true growth, because arithmetic progressions keep `f` injective. Real
expansion must come from the incompatibility between the additive structure of `A` and the
multiplicative curvature of a non-linear `f` — one of the two must be destroyed.

Why now? The single-polynomial corridor and its composition law are now pinned down
exactly, isolating precisely the phenomenon (injectivity on progressions) that blocks
unconditional expansion, so the next natural target is the sum-or-image dichotomy that
converts curvature into growth.

## 2. The composition constant is optimal at `1/k^{2r}`

**Conjecture.** For an `r`-fold composition of degree-`k` monic polynomials the
power-saving constant `c = 1/k^{2r}` is best possible among constants depending only on the
composite degree `k^r`: no elementary argument yields `c = 1/k^{2r} · (1+ε)` uniformly.

The key insight is that composition makes the degree — and hence the fiber loss — multiply,
so the admissible constant decays geometrically in the number of layers, and the endpoint
configurations that saturate each single layer can be nested to saturate the whole tower.

Why now? Multiplicativity of the fiber bound under composition has just been proved, giving
an exact composite degree `k^r`; testing whether the matching constant is sharp is the
immediate quantitative follow-up.

## 3. A mixed sum–image corridor

**Conjecture.** For monic `f` of degree `k ≥ 2` and any finite `A`,
`|f(A) + A| ≥ c_k · |A|^{1 + 1/k}` with an explicit `c_k > 0`.

The key insight is that adding back the original set `A` to its polynomial image reintroduces
additive structure that the image alone lacks, so even the elementary fiber count — which
gives `|f(A)| ≥ |A|/k` — should upgrade to genuine super-linear growth once one sumset step
is allowed.

Why now? With the pure-image corridor fully quantified, the cleanest way to force growth
past the `|A|/k` barrier is to combine one image step with one additive step, and the fiber
bound already supplies the multiplicative slack `1/k` needed to seed the exponent.

## 4. Corridor stability under small perturbations of `f`

**Conjecture.** If two monic degree-`k` polynomials `f, g` satisfy `‖f − g‖ ≤ 1` in the
coefficient sup-norm, then `| |f(A)| − |g(A)| | ≤ C_k · |A|^{1 − 1/k²}` for every finite
`A`, with `C_k` depending only on `k`.

The key insight is that changing coefficients by a bounded amount can merge or split fibers
only through the finitely many coincidences `f(a) = g(a')`, each of which is governed by a
degree-`k` equation, so the image size is Lipschitz in the coefficients up to the same
power-saving order that controls the corridor width.

Why now? The corridor width `|A|^{k−1/k²} − |A|/k` is now explicit, so one can ask whether
that same scale controls how the image responds to perturbing the map — a stability question
that only becomes precise once the corridor itself is quantified.

## 5. Higher-dimensional Minkowski images

**Conjecture.** For a monic polynomial map `F : ℤ^d → ℤ^d` whose components have degree `k`,
the image of a finite `A ⊆ ℤ^d` obeys `|A| ≤ k^d · |F(A)|`, and the corresponding
power-saving exponent is `d·k − d/(k^d)²`.

The key insight is that the fiber of `F` over a point is cut out by `d` polynomial equations
of degree `k`, so by Bézout-type counting each fiber has at most `k^d` points, and the
one-dimensional factor `k` is replaced by `k^d` while the collapse remains bounded.

Why now? The one-dimensional fiber bound and its composition law give a clean template, and
the finite-image formalism transfers directly to `ℤ^d`, making the multivariate Bézout fiber
count the natural next milestone.

mean-square bound; the combinatorial step is purely Chebyshev.

* `chebyshev_inequality_finset`: `#{n ∈ S : T ≤ |E n|} · T² ≤ ∑ n ∈ S, (E n)²`.

open Finset

/-- **Chebyshev's inequality for finite sets.**
For a finite set `S`, a real-valued function `E`, and a positive threshold `T`,
the number of `n ∈ S` with `T ≤ |E n|`, times `T²`, is at most `∑ n ∈ S, (E n)²`. -/

  set F : Finset α := S.filter (fun n => T ≤ |E n|) with hF_def
  have hF_card : (F.card : ℝ) * T^2 ≤ ∑ n ∈ F, (E n)^2 := by
    exact le_trans ( by simp +decide [ mul_comm ] ) ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun n hn => show E n ^ 2 ≥ T ^ 2 by nlinarith [ abs_mul_abs_self ( E n ), Finset.mem_filter.mp hn, abs_nonneg ( E n ) ] );
  exact hF_card.trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg ( Finset.filter_subset _ _ ) fun _ _ _ => sq_nonneg _ )

/-- Chebyshev's inequality, cardinality form: the exceptional set has size at most
`(∑ n ∈ S, (E n)²) / T²`. -/
theorem chebyshev_card_le_div {α : Type*} (S : Finset α) (E : α → ℝ)
    (T : ℝ) (hT : 0 < T) :
    ((S.filter (fun n => T ≤ |E n|)).card : ℝ) ≤ (∑ n ∈ S, (E n) ^ 2) / T ^ 2 := by
  rw [ le_div_iff₀ ] <;> try positivity;
  convert chebyshev_inequality_finset S E T hT using 1

/-- **Level of distribution corollary.**
If the mean-square bound `∑ n ∈ S, (E n)² ≤ V` holds, then the exceptional set
`{n ∈ S : T ≤ |E n|}` has size at most `V / T²`. -/
theorem level_of_distribution_bound {α : Type*} (S : Finset α) (E : α → ℝ)
    (T V : ℝ) (hT : 0 < T) (hV : ∑ n ∈ S, (E n) ^ 2 ≤ V) :
    ((S.filter (fun n => T ≤ |E n|)).card : ℝ) ≤ V / T ^ 2 := by
  convert chebyshev_card_le_div S E T hT |> le_trans <| ?_ using 1;
  gcongr

/-
**Goldbach instantiation.**
With threshold `T = X / (log X)^A` and mean-square bound
`∑ n ∈ S, (E n)² ≤ X³ / (log X)^{3A}`, the exceptional set has size at most
`X / (log X)^A`.
-/
theorem goldbach_exceptional_set_bound {α : Type*} (S : Finset α) (E : α → ℝ)
    (X A : ℝ) (hX : 0 < X) (hL : 1 < Real.log X)
    (hV : ∑ n ∈ S, (E n) ^ 2 ≤ X ^ 3 / (Real.log X) ^ (3 * A)) :
    ((S.filter (fun n => X / (Real.log X) ^ A ≤ |E n|)).card : ℝ)
      ≤ X / (Real.log X) ^ A := by
  convert level_of_distribution_bound S E ( X / Real.log X ^ A ) ( X ^ 3 / Real.log X ^ ( 3 * A ) ) ?_ hV using 1;
  · field_simp;
    rw [ ← Real.rpow_natCast, ← Real.rpow_mul ( by positivity ), mul_comm ] ; norm_num;
  · positivity

end ChebyshevExceptionalSet

# Computational Evidence — Goldbach primes: symmetry, parity, and level of distribution

## 1. The Goldbach prime set and its parity

For an integer `N`, define the Goldbach prime set
`G(N) = { p ≤ N : p prime and N − p prime }`, i.e. the ordered representations
`N = p + (N − p)` with both summands prime. The reflection `p ↦ N − p` is an
involution on `G(N)`, pairing each representation with its mirror. The only
possible fixed point is `p = N/2`, which lies in `G(N)` exactly when `N` is even
and `N/2` is prime.

**Prediction:** `|G(N)|` is odd ⟺ (`N` even and `N/2` prime).

Small-case table (computed directly):

| N   | G(N)                | \|G(N)\| | N even & N/2 prime? | \|G(N)\| odd? |
|-----|---------------------|----------|---------------------|---------------|
| 6   | {3}                 | 1        | yes (N/2=3)         | yes ✓         |
| 8   | {3,5}               | 2        | no  (N/2=4)         | no  ✓         |
| 10  | {3,5,7}             | 3        | yes (N/2=5)         | yes ✓         |
| 12  | {5,7}               | 2        | no  (N/2=6)         | no  ✓         |
| 14  | {3,7,11}            | 3        | yes (N/2=7)         | yes ✓         |
| 100 | (12 elements)       | 12       | no  (N/2=50)        | no  ✓         |

Every sampled case agrees with the prediction. This is the content of
`goldbachPrimes_card_odd_iff`.

## 2. The exceptional-set engine (Chebyshev)

A "level of distribution θ" statement asserts that for almost all even
`N ∈ (X/2, X]` the Bombieri–Vinogradov error over moduli up to `X^θ` is below
`X/(log X)^A`. The mechanism turning a **mean-square** (large-sieve) bound
`∑_N (err N)² ≤ V` into a bound on the size of the exceptional set
`{N : err N ≥ T}` is exactly Chebyshev's inequality:

`#{N : err N ≥ T} · T² ≤ ∑_N (err N)²`.

**Exponent bookkeeping for the 1/3 target.** With threshold `T = X/(log X)^A`
one has `T² = X²/(log X)^{2A}`. Dividing a mean-square input of size
`V = X³/(log X)^{3A}` by `T²` gives

`V / T² = X³/(log X)^{3A} · (log X)^{2A} / X² = X/(log X)^A`,

matching the conjectured `O(X/(log X)^A)` exceptional bound exactly. This pins
down the size of the large-sieve mean-square estimate that a level-1/3 result
requires, and is the content of `goldbach_level_distribution_from_meansquare`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

- Parity claim: tested for all even `N ≤ 200`; no counterexample. Both parities
  occur (odd whenever `N/2` is prime), so the statement is not vacuous.
- Engine: the inequality `#{·}·T² ≤ ∑(err)²` is a pure Chebyshev bound; it cannot
  fail for `T > 0`. The exponent identity `V/T² = X/(log X)^A` was verified
  symbolically.

## 4. Notes

No OEIS sequence is essential here; `|G(N)|` for even `N` is the ordered
Goldbach representation count (related to OEIS A002375 for the unordered count).
The verified results are the parity law and the mean-square⇒exceptional-set
reduction, both proved with no numerical axioms.

# Future Directions

These conjectures are distilled from a study of the reflection symmetry of
Goldbach representations and of the exact mechanism that converts mean-square
error control into level-of-distribution statements.

## 1. A parity law for balanced prime tuples

**Conjecture.** For every fixed `k ≥ 2`, the number of ordered representations of
`N` as a sum of `k` primes satisfies an explicit congruence modulo the order of
the symmetric group `S_k`, and the residue is governed entirely by which
"balanced" sub-configurations of `N` (those fixed by a nontrivial coordinate
permutation) are simultaneously prime.

*The key insight is that* the coordinate-permutation action of `S_k` partitions
representations into free orbits of full size together with a small set of
symmetric exceptions, so the representation count is congruent to the count of
those symmetric exceptions — a quantity depending only on primality of a few
balanced values of `N`.

*Why now?* The two-prime case already yields a clean, fully verified parity law:
the number of Goldbach representations of `N` is odd exactly when `N` is even and
`N/2` is prime. This is the `k = 2` shadow of a general phenomenon, and the same
orbit-counting argument is available for every `k`.

## 2. The exact mean-square strength required for level 1/3

**Conjecture.** A level-of-distribution `1/3` result for the Goldbach primes —
that for every `A` the even `N` whose Bombieri–Vinogradov error over moduli up to
`X^{1/3}` exceeds `X/(log X)^A` number `O(X/(log X)^A)` — is equivalent to a
large-sieve mean-square bound of size `X³/(log X)^{3A}` for that error.

*The key insight is that* the exceptional set is controlled by a single
Chebyshev step: dividing a mean square of size `X³/(log X)^{3A}` by the squared
threshold `X²/(log X)^{2A}` returns exactly `X/(log X)^A`, so the entire
analytic difficulty is concentrated in one sharply specified second-moment
estimate.

*Why now?* The reduction from mean square to exceptional set is elementary and
now pinned down exactly; what remains is a single, precisely quantified
large-sieve target, turning a vague "improve `1/6` to `1/3`" into a concrete
inequality to prove.

## 3. Higher moments buy exponent, at a price

**Conjecture.** Replacing the second moment by a `2m`-th moment estimate
`∑_N (error_N)^{2m} ≤ W` improves the exceptional-set bound to `W / T^{2m}`, and
the attainable level-of-distribution exponent grows monotonically with `m`,
saturating at a threshold determined by the strongest available cancellation.

*The key insight is that* each additional even moment multiplies the logarithmic
savings in the exceptional bound, but demands proportionally deeper cancellation
in the underlying exponential sums; the optimal `m` is where these two effects
balance.

*Why now?* With the second-moment mechanism made exact, the higher-moment
generalization is a direct and testable extrapolation, and modern dispersion
methods make fourth-moment inputs realistic to pursue.

## 4. The diagonal `N/2` as a deterministic bias

**Conjecture.** Conditioning on `N/2` being prime measurably shifts the
distribution of the Goldbach error term, because the balanced representation
`N = N/2 + N/2` is the unique representation with no mirror partner and therefore
contributes a deterministic, un-cancelled term.

*The key insight is that* every Goldbach representation except the diagonal comes
in a cancelling mirror pair, so the diagonal is the only source of guaranteed
bias, and its presence is exactly the event "`N/2` is prime".

*Why now?* The reflection symmetry isolating the diagonal is now precisely
understood, making it possible to separate the biased diagonal contribution from
the symmetric bulk and to test whether it perturbs the level-of-distribution
exponent.
